title: PineRiver Console request tracing & error playbook walkthrough
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked PineRiver team through the Console request tracing, request logs, and error analysis playbook. Focus on correlating request IDs across services, KV cache fallthroughs, model fallback behavior, and SSO/audit log requirements. Action items: run a 1k-request replay with Redwood sandbox, share security whitepaper, and schedule a dedicated latency deep-dive with PineRiver infra team.
topics: KV cache miss patterns and fallbacks
Error triage workflow and root-cause correlation
Demo: request replayer + trace link handoff

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-30
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Mills (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Mark Liu (PineRiver - Head of ML), Sara Bennett (PineRiver - SRE), Tomas Rivera (PineRiver - CTO)

Auto-summary: Quick demo of console tracing features, playback, and error analysis. Discussed how to tie request IDs from PineRiver's EKS logs to Redwood's request traces and strategies for KV cache fallthroughs and model fallback auditing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, um, quick roll call?
[00:08] Mark (PineRiver): Mark here, hi.
[00:10] Sara (PineRiver): Sara, hi.
[00:12] Tomas (PineRiver): Tomas, good afternoon.
[00:14] Jordan: great. Priya from our SE team is with me, she'll take most of the console walkthrough and the trace deep-dive.
[00:20] Priya (Redwood SE): hi all, excited to walk through how you can use the request playback and the trace correlator to debug errors end-to-end.
[00:28] Mark: quick context — we're running an EKS cluster in us-east-1 with a sidecar that emits request_id headers, and our infra team has noticed intermittent 5xx spikes around midnight. They're wondering if this is model latency, cache thrash, or network flakiness.
[00:45] Priya: perfect, that's exactly the scenario the Console trace correlator helps with. We'll show how to map your sidecar request_id to Redwood request IDs and then walk the whole token-level latency and error waterfall.
[00:58] Sara: we also need detailed audit logs for SOC2 — retention, KMS, and who accessed what. We'll want to see how the console surfaces that.
[01:08] Jordan: yup, we'll show the audit panel and how RBAC maps to your SAML groups. quick note, security docs are in the folder we'll share afterwards.
[01:18] Priya: ok I'm sharing my screen — starting at the Requests table. you'll notice request rows with durations, model variant, and a small trace link. if you click the trace you get a timeline of events — request ingress, batching, model selection, kv cache hit/miss, and response.
[01:35] [02:15] Priya: here's a sample request — notice this one has a KV miss flagged at step 3, then a model fallback from the 70b fp16 quantized to the 13b fallback because of resource contention, that change is highlighted. you can expand the token timeline to see which tokens were slow.
[02:45] Mark: when you say kv miss, is that our prefix cache or the runtime-level kv? we have both — the sidecar prefix cache and Redwood's kv cache. sometimes they overlap and it's confusing.
[03:00] Priya: good question. the console shows both: the header "prefix cache" and the runtime "KV cache (serve)". sometimes the transcription here says K-V cash which is annoying, but it's the runtime KV. you can filter to only show runtime cache events.
[03:17] Sara: can we correlate the request to our k8s pod logs? like link to the pod name or kube request id?
[03:25] Priya: yes — in the tenant settings you can add a correlation key. we recommended you inject the pine_river_request_id into the outbound header; Redwood will persist it on the trace and search for it. we'll demo that with a sample that Mark will provide.
[03:40] Tomas: another pain is replaying a failing session. will the playback respect model fallbacks and exact token timing? we need fidelity for debug.
[03:50] Priya: playback is deterministic to model variant and prompt, but timing can be adjusted. the replayer has two modes: fidelity — which preserves original rate and model selection — and stress — which replays at faster rates to reproduce concurrency issues.
[04:05] Jordan: and we also capture the exact model version and quantization profile so you can see whether a quantized kernel induced an error.
[04:14] [05:00] Mark: interesting. on the spikes we saw, our telemetry shows an increased number of cache evictions. could Redwood's autoscaling kick in and trigger fallbacks?
[04:23] Priya: autoscaling shouldn't trigger a different model variant, but if capacity is constrained and we route to a lower-tier instance, the platform can apply a fallback policy you configure — e.g. degrade to a cheaper model or queue requests. we'll show the routing policy panel after traces.
[04:40] Sara: for compliance we need immutable audit logs tied to request ids. if someone deletes a trace in the console, we still need an audit trail. how do you handle that?
[04:52] Priya: deletion is soft for analytics, and audit logs are shipped to your KMS-encrypted archive if you enable the enterprise retention add-on. we can set write-once retention windows. we'll attach our security whitepaper and the retention config options.
[05:10] [06:12] Priya: moving to an example trace — see this session with repeated 502s. the timeline shows network timeouts to the model host at token 12, then a fallback. the console groups events by service — ingress sidecar, backend router, model shard.
[05:30] Mark: the trace shows "router timeout 504" but our pod logs show a 200 on the sidecar. is there a mismatch?
[05:38] Priya: sometimes sidecar logs are emitted before the final code path, or timestamp skew happens. the console attempts to align by converting to server time and we'll show how to overlay your cluster logs by uploading a small mapping file.
[05:52] Tomas: are timestamps normalized to UTC? we have a global team.
[05:55] Priya: yes UTC in the console timeline, with an option to view local tz.
[06:04] [07:20] Jordan: let's talk about anomaly detection — you can pin a golden latency profile and get alerted when shape changes occur; but for root cause you still use the trace-to-log correlation.
[06:28] Sara: does anomaly detection learn from our traffic patterns and ignore scheduled batch jobs? we get a nightly batch that spikes requests.
[06:38] Priya: you can add a rule to exclude scheduled namespaces or IP ranges. also the model-level aggregator ignores known synthetic traffic if you tag it at ingestion.
[06:50] Mark: ok show us a full replay? I've uploaded a small sample of 25 failing requests in the shared folder.
[07:00] Priya: loading those now. starting the replay — choosing fidelity mode. note the replayer has a trace link on each replayed request so you can step into the exact event sequence.
[07:18] [08:05] Priya: here's one of the replays — you can see the playback timeline on the right, and a diff view comparing successful vs failing requests token-by-token. see token 9 where the model stalls; there's also a corresponding spike in our runtime metric for memory pressure.
[07:40] Mark: that memory pressure spike, does it correlate with a particular kernel? like attention implementation?
[07:46] Priya: it can. the console surfaces kernel selection notes where available — e.g., fused attention vs standard — but note that in some older models that metadata might be sparse. we can run a model-level profiler if you want deeper kernel traces.
[08:05] [09:30] Sara: how long do request logs live by default? we anticipate needing 90 days for audits.
[08:12] Jordan: default is 30 days for request payloads and 90 for aggregated metrics, but enterprise plans can extend raw request retention to your desired window with encrypted archiving.
[08:22] Sara: and is payload encryption using customer-managed KMS keys possible?
[08:25] Priya: yes, customer-managed KMS is an option on Private or Dedicated; for Hosted we offer a bring-your-key workflow for enterprise tenants.
[08:38] [10:25] Mark: competitor question — we evaluated Anthropic's console, their trace links seemed less granular. how do you compare?
[08:45] Jordan: without naming too many specifics, our differentiator is token-level timelines, model variant lineage, and built-in playback that preserves model configuration. that combination is the main thing folks pick Redwood for.
[08:58] [11:00] Tomas: ok, from an ops perspective, can we export traces into our SIEM? we use Splunk and Datadog.
[11:06] Priya: yes — exports to S3, and direct streaming to Splunk/Datadog via our logging connectors. we can push structured trace JSON that includes your correlation key.
[11:19] Sara: does streaming add latency or cost?
[11:22] Priya: negligible latency on the request path — exports run asynchronously. there is cost for high retention and streaming throughput but we can size it predictably.
[11:34] [12:40] Mark: earlier you mentioned routing policies — can we set a canary so that 5% of traffic uses a new model and automatically fallback if error rate > threshold?
[12:48] Priya: absolutely — rollouts support traffic weights, per-route success thresholds, and automatic rollback. you'll see both the original and canary traces side-by-side in the console.
[12:58] Jordan: I want to call out how trace links are included in the SDK responses as X-Redwood-Trace. if you log that in your sidecar, it immediately appears in the console and you can search by it.
[13:14] [14:45] Priya: quick demo of the error analysis panel — it aggregates errors by type, shows top stack traces where available, and lets you jump to a failing request to start a replay. there are also automated suggestions — e.g., tune batch size, increase prefix cache TTL, or change quantization profile. the suggestions are heuristics.
[14:30] Mark: those heuristics, are they based on our traffic or global heuristics?
[14:35] Priya: a mix — they start from global best practices but the console refines them using your tenant metrics over time.
[14:44] [16:10] Sara: if we want to keep traces private on-prem, is there an offline mode for the console? we can't send certain PII off-network.
[16:17] Priya: for on-prem/private deployments we ship a private console that you deploy into your VPC; traces never leave your network. for hosted customers we mask PII by default and recommend syntactic filters.
[16:30] Tomas: what's the onboarding effort like? how long to get correlation keys wired in production?
[16:36] Jordan: for teams with a sidecar it can be minutes to hours — usually one small header change then a short smoke test. for full audit and retention config with KMS it takes a bit longer—we can walk your infra team through the steps.
[16:50] [18:00] Priya: ok, jumping into a live troubleshooting example we prepared — the failing requests you uploaded show an interesting pattern: retries from the client at the same second followed by model OOMs. in the trace you can see the OOM event logged as "model shard alloc fail".
[18:16] Mark: OOMs would line up with our cache eviction spikes perhaps. is there guidance for KV cache sizing?
[18:24] Priya: yes, Optimize gives recommendations for cache TTL and object sizing based on sequence length distribution. it ties directly into the console so you can applied suggested changes and re-run replays to measure impact.
[18:40] [20:05] Jordan: we should also note fallback transparency — the console shows a lineage view: original request -> attempted model -> applied fallback -> final response. everything is auditable.
[19:00] Sara: can we redact prompts in traces for compliance? some prompts contain PHI-like examples for testing.
[19:06] Priya: yes there are redaction rules — you can pre-process requests or use field-level masking in the Console settings.
